questions.prompt: An LP commits $100M, pays in $80M, receives $40M in distributions, and the remaining portfolio NAV is $120M. What is the TVPI?
questions.explanation: TVPI = (Distributions + NAV) / Paid-In = ($40M + $120M) / $80M = $160M / $80M = 2.00x. DPI = 0.50x and RVPI = 1.50x.

questions.prompt: What is the key mathematical distinction between KS-PME and Long-Nickels PME?
choices: KS-PME uses IRR while LN-PME uses a market multiple
LN-PME uses IRR and can create a synthetic short; KS-PME uses a market multiple by discounting cash flows
KS-PME is only applicable to co-investments; LN-PME applies to primaries
They are mathematically identical but output different units
questions.explanation: LN-PME simulates selling index shares for distributions, which can create a synthetic short for highly performant funds, breaking the IRR. KS-PME fixes this by discounting all contributions and distributions by the index return to produce a clean market multiple.

questions.prompt: Describe the synergistic relationship between NB's Primaries team and Co-Investment team within the PIPCO architecture. Why is this integration considered a core competitive advantage?
questions.modelAnswer: The Primaries team acts as the top of the information funnel. By committing $40+ billion to hundreds of GPs globally, it builds deep institutional relationships and gains access to proprietary deal flow data. When a GP originates a transaction too large for its own fund, it syndicates the excess equity to trusted primary LPs as co-investments. The Co-investment team receives priority access to these transactions without broker fees. Conversely, by performing rigorous bottom-up underwriting on live GP deals, the Co-investment team provides the Primaries group with real-time empirical insight into a GP's current pricing discipline and operational acumen — directly informing whether NB will re-commit to that GP's next fund. This bidirectional feedback loop creates an information advantage that standalone primaries-only or co-investment-only platforms cannot replicate.

questions.prompt: Walk through the PCAP roll-forward equation and explain why each component matters for an analyst reconciling quarterly reports.
questions.modelAnswer: The PCAP roll-forward: Ending NAV = Beginning NAV + Capital Called − Distributions + Realized Gains + Unrealized Gains/Losses − Management Fees/Expenses. Capital Called increases the LP's invested position when the GP draws down committed capital. Distributions reduce NAV as realized proceeds are returned to the LP. Realized Gains capture profits from actual exits. Unrealized Gains/Losses reflect fair-value changes in unsold portfolio companies (the largest source of quarterly movement). Management Fees/Expenses reduce NAV as the cost of running the fund is charged to LPs. An analyst reconciles this equation against data in Burgiss to confirm the GP's accounting is accurate — any imbalance signals an error in either the PCAP or the internal system, triggering an inquiry to fund administration.
